title: The Curious Case of Ketamine: Is Less Often More Effective?
subtitle: New research findings in collaboration with Dr. Irfan Handoo challenge my understanding of Ketamine
body_html:
Dr. Irfan Handoo is a brilliant physician who lives in Kansas City. He works very hard. He's dedicated to his patients' well-being to a degree might boggle the imagination of most. I've been pleased to know Irfan for several years, and we've worked together on at six publications already. I wasn't ready for my colleague upending my understanding of how IV Ketamine should be delivered.

If you want to see Dr. Handoo, here is the link:

Visit Kansas City Psychiatry Partners

Except— that's what happened.

The conversation started when Dr. Handoo told my co-author, Amna Aslam, MPH, about his data on ketamine.

Handoo’s TMS data was exciting enough: together, we had a whole series of patients who had been previously treated with ECT, and ketamine, and regular rTMS, and whose depression subsequently remitted with dTMS1— a variant of the technology using a different coil geometry, both broader and deeper than the figure-of-eight coils first demonstrated effective in 2008. We looked at our data here at Radial and found we also had several such patients. We pulled that data and published a case series in the Journal of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation. Here's the summary:

For those who don't get relief from all theoretically “best” treatments, there is yet another option that works. It seems similar, but our data suggest dTMS is meaningfully different for certain subgroups.

Inspiring — more hope! That paper is out the door. However, my socks were knocked even further off next, when I saw the data Handoo had regarding the use of intravenous ketamine.

Traditionally, ketamine has been administered twice to thrice weekly, throughout six infusions over two or three weeks. The dosing has been either 0.5 mg per kilogram or more, depending on the whims of whoever was administering the treatment. People who were trained in anesthesia tended to use higher dosages because they were familiar with managing them, and psychiatrists tend to use lower dosages because they were comfortable with the first thing they learned.

Dr. Handoo understood that a different way to administer this protocol might allow for more personalization. The idea is that the dose-response curve of ketamine might have an “inverted U-shaped” to reach an optimal dosage.

I'll draw that for you:

So helpful, I know. Oh, you know what I can make it even more helpful:

There is a sweet spot. For any person, there is an optimal dosage in milligrams per kilogram. Above that, the effect gets worse, and below that, the effect isn't good enough. This isn't a particularly controversial idea in most of medicine. We established blood levels of lithium for example. One can have too much or too little of a drug, and it won't work very well compared to optimal dosing. Water, for the purposes of hydration, follows similar rules.

However, for the use of ketamine and depression, this dose-response curve had not been established in advance. One of the reasons it was difficult to establish a meaningful response curve is that the rating scale we use cannot measure change quickly. All the questions in the PHQ-9, for example, assume depression can’t change faster than every two weeks:

It says, up top—OVER THE LAST TWO WEEKS. This assumption—that depression couldn’t change more rapidly—created a measurement tool that is non-functional for measuring rapidly improving depression.

According to this measurement standard, improving faster than two weeks is impossible. It is as if we were trying to measure the height of an ant with a meter stick, and with no subdivisions. Ants are shorter than a meter. Thus, it would be highly error-prone to attempt that measurement with that stick. Similarly, it would be a problem if my readership was only measured in units of millions. I have approximately zero readers in those units.

You get the point. Dr. Handoo modified this standard form in one crucial way: he asked the patients who were getting the ketamine all the same questions, but as it had been applied over the past week. He then adjusted the next dose of IV ketamine for his patients, which was only once a week, based on the prior weeks’ response on the modified PHQ-9. If the patients improved, his protocol dose escalated (in mg/kg). If the patient got worse, his protocol reduced the dose. He realized it was possible to overshoot a dose of this medicine, in keeping with the theorized inverted-U shape of the curve.

With traditionally IV Ketamine dosing, done 2-3 times a week over 2 weeks, the clinician can’t adjust to changes in the response, thanks to the “glitch” in the PHQ-9. IV Ketamine, thusly dosed, is already an effective treatment, as demonstrated by extensive real-world data sets, such as those published by McInnes and colleagues:

Among the 537 patients who underwent induction and had sufficient data, 53.6% of patients showed a response (≥ 50% reduction in PHQ-9 score) at 14–31 days post-induction and 28.9% remitted (PHQ-9 score drop to < 5). The effect size was d = 1.5. Among patients with baseline suicidal ideation (SI), 73.0% exhibited a reduction in SI. A subset (8.4%) of patients experienced an increase in depressive symptoms after induction while 6.0% of patients reported increased SI.2

As you can see above, the remission rate was south of 30%, and some patients did worse, consistent with Dr. Handoo’s hypothesis. However, Dr. Handoo theorized we were leaving better outcomes “on the table” if we didn't optimize the dose. He relentlessly collected data. First 10, the 100, and now several hundred have been treated with this approach.

Here is the poster we have accepted to the APA annual meeting. It’s only reporting on a randomized fraction of the total data, as we didn’t have access to the whole data set after he switched institutions).

The results?

Flexibly-dosed weekly ketamine got 57% of patients to remission in this open-label sample.

To determine true superiority, a direct comparison RCT with 2-3x week dosing would be necessary, and would have to be a very large sample. However, 57% remission is more than 28.9%, by a non trivial amount, especially given this is the same drug we are talking about.

Stay tuned for my upcoming podcast episodes with Dr Irfan Handoo!

2

McInnes, L. A., Qian, J. J., Gargeya, R. S., DeBattista, C., & Heifets, B. D. (2022). A retrospective analysis of ketamine intravenous therapy for depression in real-world care settings. Journal of Affective Disorders, 301, 486-495.
